title: The Base64 Feature's Nearest Neuron
takeaway: The MLP neuron whose activations track the base64 feature most closely, A/neurons/470, correlates with it at only 0.18, and its own activation distribution stays mostly blue — mostly non-base64 — at every activation level. Its sampled examples are code, XML namespaces, pandoc `label="…"` markup, URL fragments and citation keys, categories with nothing in common but a punctuation-heavy texture. The paper reads this as the feature not being a neuron in disguise.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A/neurons/470 is an actual MLP neuron inside transformer A, not one of the [[feature]] directions the autoencoder learned. The paper found it by scanning roughly 40 million dataset examples for the neuron whose activations track the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 most closely. That search is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] check.

The plot is the [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]] used earlier for the feature itself, redrawn for the neuron so the two shapes can be compared.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the neuron's activation on a token, running from just above $0$ to about $7.2$. Hard zeros are excluded — sparsity would put a spike at zero that dwarfs everything else — and the small "0 / >0" control at bottom left is that switch. The vertical axis is density, the number of tokens landing in each activation bin, peaking near 1.4M just above zero.

Color carries a second variable. Each token gets a [[base64-proxy]] score, the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log\big(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s)\big)$, which is large and positive for strings that look like random base64 and negative for ordinary text. The legend runs from $-5$ (blue) to $+5$ (red). Within each vertical slice the tokens are stacked reddest-at-the-bottom. The thin strip beneath the main plot is the same stack renormalized to full height, so proportions stay readable where the raw density has fallen to nothing.

The four boxes are random dataset examples drawn from the activation levels marked by the dotted leader lines. Orange shading shows the neuron's activation per token; the bold token is the sampled one, with four tokens of context on each side.

### What it shows

Dark red never takes over. It stays a thin band along the bottom at every activation level, including the far right. The same plot for A/1/2357 is essentially solid red above roughly activation 4.

The samples say why. One box holds a PHP error, a JSON `"slug":null`, and `{data-label="tabest"}`. Another holds an XML namespace, a wiki URL and a citation key `[@bib43]`. A third is figure labels and `\[subsect:Moment\]`. The top box, near activation 6.7, is nothing but `label="…"}` markup and citation keys.

No visible sample is base64, though the paper says the neuron does respond to base64 notably. The categories share no meaning, only a machine-written, punctuation-dense texture.

The [[pearson-correlation]] between neuron and feature is 0.18, against 0.85 for the feature's counterpart in the second run. The neuron carries some base64 and much else — [[polysemanticity]], the outcome [[superposition]] predicts, and the thing this whole check exists to rule out for the learned features.

terms.definition: The plot title. It means a histogram over the ~100M-token visualization corpus of how often this unit takes each activation value, here broken down by color into how base64-like the underlying token was.

Neuron number 470 in the MLP layer of transformer A. The `neurons` slot in the paper's naming scheme marks this as a real unit of the transformer rather than a direction learned by a dictionary-learning run.

The base64 feature this neuron is being compared against: feature 2357 from dictionary-learning run 1 on transformer A. It is not drawn in this figure, but the 0.18 in the caption is its correlation with the neuron.
The label for the row of four text boxes above the plot. Each box holds random dataset examples sampled from one slice of the neuron's activation range, not the top-activating examples.
The vertical axis: how many tokens in the sampled corpus fall into each activation bin. It is a raw count, which is why it reaches millions.
The horizontal axis: the value the neuron outputs on a given token. Higher means the neuron fired harder on that token.

The color legend's title. Each token is scored by $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$ — how much more likely the surrounding string is under a random-base64 model than under the paper's unigram model of ordinary text.
The hypothesis the color scale tests. The paper models a base64 string as a random sequence over the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/], the encoding used to embed binary data inside text.

The stacking key. Blue tokens score low on the base64 proxy (ordinary text), red tokens score high (base64-like). Inside each vertical slice the reddest tokens are stacked at the bottom, so a red band hugging the axis is the base64-like share.

The small control at the bottom left of the axis. The plot shows only nonzero activations; because the unit is off for most tokens, including exact zeros would produce a spike at 0 that flattens the rest of the curve.

The short band below the main plot. It is the same color stack with every column stretched to full height, so the proportion of base64-like tokens stays legible out in the tail where the raw density is near zero.
The four vertical dotted lines connecting each example box to the activation level its examples were drawn from — roughly 1.05, 2.15, 4.3 and 6.7.
Inside an example box, the background shade on each token shows how strongly the neuron activated there. Darker orange means a larger activation.
The token that was actually sampled at that activation level. The paper shows four tokens of context on either side of it.
Shorthand in the caption for the Pearson correlation between the neuron's activation and the feature's activation, computed token-by-token over a large sample of dataset examples.
One sampled example: an XML namespace declaration. It is markup plus a URL, and represents the "code and HTML labels" category the caption names.
Sampled examples of pandoc-style attribute markup used to label figures and tables in converted academic documents. These dominate the neuron's highest activation bin.
Sampled examples of citation keys in pandoc/BibTeX-converted text. Another unrelated category the neuron fires on.
A sampled example from a PHP error message. It stands for the general "code" category the caption lists.

Sampled examples from a JSON blob and a hexadecimal-looking identifier. The hex-like strings matter because the base64 proxy scores them high even though the paper says a separate feature, A/1/3817, handles hexadecimal.
A sampled example that is a fragment of a URL path — the "parts of URLs" category from the caption.
A sampled example of an escaped LaTeX-style cross-reference in converted text. It is neither code nor base64, and shows how wide the neuron's response range is.

numbers.meaning: The index of the neuron in transformer A's MLP layer. It has no meaning beyond identification; the paper selected it because it was the neuron most correlated with the base64 feature, not because of where it sits.

The Pearson correlation between A/neurons/470's activations and A/1/2357's activations. This is the highest such correlation over all neurons in the model, so 0.18 is a ceiling, not a typical value — no neuron tracks this feature closely.

For contrast, from the preceding subsection: the correlation between A/1/2357 and its counterpart feature B/1/2165 in a second, independently trained model. A feature in another model matches far better than the best neuron in the same model.

From the same case study: the correlation between A/1/2357 and the base64 proxy itself. The paper attributes the low value to the proxy being too broad — hexadecimal strings, for example, score high on it but belong to a different feature.
The index of the base64 feature within dictionary-learning run A/1. Feature indices are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder.

The ticks on the Log-Likelihood Ratio color legend, in log units. Zero means the string is equally likely under the base64 model and under the ordinary-text unigram model; +5 means about $e^5$ times more likely under base64; -5 the reverse. The scale is clipped at these ends.
The density axis ticks, counting tokens per activation bin. The scale reaches millions because this neuron is active on a large share of tokens.
The peak density, at the smallest nonzero activation bin. The distribution falls monotonically from there, the ordinary shape for a unit that mostly fires weakly.

The range of the activation axis, so roughly 7.2 is the largest activation this neuron reaches in the sample. The feature A/1/2357's own plot runs out to about 12.5, so the neuron's dynamic range is narrower.

The peak density on the corresponding plot for the feature A/1/2357 — about thirty-five times smaller than this neuron's 1.4M peak. The feature fires on far fewer tokens, which is what the sparsity penalty is buying.

The activation level above which the feature A/1/2357's version of this plot is essentially solid red. This neuron's plot never reaches that state at any level, which is the contrast the figure is making.

The four activation levels the dotted leader lines mark, and from which the example boxes were sampled. They spread across the range so a reader can see whether the neuron's meaning sharpens as it fires harder. Here it does not.
Two things: the number of example boxes, and the number of context tokens shown on each side of the sampled token in every snippet.
The size of the token subset from the training data used to build these visualizations, with only 10 tokens taken from each context so the samples are not dominated by a few documents.
The number of dataset examples over which the paper computed activation correlations when searching for the neuron most correlated with a feature.
The probability the base64 proxy assigns to each of the 64 characters in [a-zA-Z0-9+/] under the base64 hypothesis, treating a base64 string as uniform random over that alphabet.
The probability the base64 proxy assigns to any character outside the base64 alphabet. It is a near-zero floor rather than exactly zero so the log-likelihood ratio stays finite.
